This page covers the exact U.S. O*NET/SOC occupation 25-2031.00, Secondary School Teachers, Except Special and Career/Technical Education: teaching one or more subjects to students at the secondary school level. Official scope: Teach one or more subjects to students at the secondary school level. O*NET lists core tasks including the following (the page lists 32 tasks and displays the first 5 by default): preparing students for later grades by encouraging exploration of learning opportunities and perseverance with challenging tasks; teaching subjects such as English, mathematics or social studies through lectures, discussions and demonstrations; establishing and enforcing student behavior rules and procedures for maintaining order; preparing materials and classrooms for activities; and adapting teaching methods and materials to varying student needs and interests. Common job titles include High School Teacher, Secondary Teacher, Math Teacher, English Teacher, Science Teacher and Social Studies Teacher. Coverage note: U.S. wage and employment data presented on O*NET's 25-2031.00 page are not marked as coming from a broader or neighboring occupation, so this page identifies them as data for this occupation itself (25-2031.00). In the U.S., it is in Job Zone Four (considerable preparation needed), 7.0 to less than 8.0 (SVP 7.0 to < 8.0). This page does not extrapolate U.S. classifications to job titles, qualifications or wages in mainland China.

Practice brief | A wholly fictional instructional design task package (for practicing the process only; it does not represent any real school, class or data). Draft a plan explaining: (1) how to use fictional curriculum standards and student learning information to design a unit systematically, covering subject, grade and unit topic, learning goals and observable performance, prerequisites and common misconceptions, activity, lecture, discussion and demonstration arrangements, differentiated materials and support, assessment tasks and rubrics, classroom order, safety and timing, homework, feedback and subsequent adjustments; identify missing information needing clarification, including curriculum standard and textbook versions, student learning and special needs, school, examination and safety requirements, available technology and resources and data permissions; (2) how to design completion and review points for a fictional student learning record, covering fields and definitions, learning goals and evidence, assignments, assessments and rubrics, feedback and improvement, abnormalities, support and referrals, record trails and privacy boundaries; (3) how to write a unit teaching summary suitable for handover, covering goals—activities—assessment evidence—student performance—adjustments and next steps; (4) how to retain and use student data and distinguish public information from protected student personal information and grades; and (5) how to pause, review, report and hand over when laboratory or activity safety, bullying, psychological crisis or data breach risks, matters beyond authorization or safety risks are identified. Use public sources and simulated data, without real school or student data.

Fit signals | U.S. O*NET 25-2031.00 has interest code S (Social, Social: centered on teaching, helping, advising, assisting or serving others). Core activities include training and teaching others, communicating with supervisors, peers, or subordinates, organizing, planning and prioritizing work, making decisions and solving problems, getting information and interpreting information for others. Work context indicates frequent face-to-face discussions in classroom teaching and instructional collaboration, close collaboration with colleagues, parents and administrators, frequent daily decisions through immediate classroom adjustments and assessment judgments, high assessment accuracy requirements, time pressure from lessons, examinations and grading milestones, and substantial communication with students, parents and communities. If you are willing to work directly with students, subjects and classrooms, develop sound learning goals, activities, assessments and feedback, and take responsibility for student development, assessment fairness and classroom safety, daily demands may be closer to your working style.

Caution signals | O*NET also indicates, for 25-2031.00 work context and tasks, time pressure from lessons, examinations and grading milestones; evening and weekend work varying by school and duties; serious consequences from erroneous or biased assessments and safety omissions; substantial responsibility for student health and safety; possible chemical and equipment hazards during laboratories and activities; and moderate disease or infection exposure in densely populated schools. This occupation works with students, subjects, classrooms and assessment. A biased or unfair assessment, inadequate laboratory or activity safety plan, student privacy or data breach, or missed bullying or psychological crisis signal may harm students and create home-school conflict, liability and compliance risks. O*NET places it in Job Zone Four (considerable preparation needed), 7.0 to less than 8.0 (SVP 7.0 to < 8.0). Its education section reports that 77% indicate a bachelor's degree is required, 8% a post-baccalaureate certificate, and 8% a post-master's certificate (the three categories listed). Growth is labeled Decline (-1% or lower), without Bright Outlook. If sustained lesson, examination and home-school communication workloads are difficult, or evening and weekend work is difficult to accept, or you are unwilling to take responsibility for student development, assessment fairness and classroom safety, treat these as practical costs.

Responsibility judgment | Real fit depends on whether you can do three things within the same teaching assignment: deliver sound teaching by developing goals, activities, assessments, feedback and records according to curriculum standards and student learning needs, producing usable learning evidence and teaching records; manage safety, compliance and boundaries by working and keeping records according to activity safety, campus emergency, student privacy, data minimization and internal reporting-chain requirements, distinguishing public information from protected student personal information and grades and handling them under procedures, and avoiding unauthorized actions, evaluations or disclosures beyond your remit; and accept defined responsibility for your own teaching goals, curriculum delivery, assessment and records, while referring matters beyond authorization or involving psychological crises, safety or law to appropriate roles or organizations under procedures. Test this through a verifiable experience, such as a teaching plan and assessment and record explanation for a fictional unit, or a review of laboratory, bullying or data security abnormality handling, rather than relying only on an interest questionnaire.

Direct answer | This page's Secondary School Teachers, Except Special and Career/Technical Education is the exact O*NET occupation 25-2031.00. Work falls into several categories: (I) goals and curriculum—defining learning goals and observable performance according to curriculum standards, preparing students for later grades, and adapting teaching methods and materials to varying needs and interests; (II) teaching delivery—teaching one or more subjects through lectures, discussions and demonstrations, preparing materials and classrooms for activities, and establishing and enforcing student behavior rules and procedures for maintaining order; (III) assessment and feedback—assigning and grading homework and assessments, providing rubric-based feedback and adjusting teaching according to student performance; (IV) student support and collaboration—identifying learning, behavioral and emotional needs and providing support or referrals under procedures, and collaborating with students, parents, colleagues and administrators; and (V) records and professional development—recording learning progress, attendance and assessment evidence, participating in instructional collaboration and training, and updating professional knowledge.

Boundary conclusion | This page covers O*NET 25-2031.00, Secondary School Teachers, Except Special and Career/Technical Education. The central distinction from neighboring roles concerns student developmental stage, subject depth and responsibility boundaries. This occupation teaches one or more academic subjects to secondary-level students, specializing by subject and producing evidence of academic development and teaching and assessment records. Elementary teachers, middle school teachers, special education teachers, career/technical education teachers and education administrators differ in educational stage, specialty and authority and are not interchangeable by title.

Core principle of neighboring roles | Most related and neighboring roles aim to deliver teaching, support or management according to curriculum standards and student development requirements, with records retained. Differences concern student developmental stage, subject depth, specialist support and authorization levels: some focus on secondary academic subjects, others on elementary or middle school, special education, career/technical education or school management.

Core purpose of this occupation | Work with secondary-level students, academic subjects and curriculum standards within teaching qualifications and school authorization: goals and curriculum, classroom delivery, assessment and feedback, student support and collaboration, and records and professional development. Outputs are evidence of academic development and traceable teaching and assessment records.

Main work objects and bases of neighboring roles | Elementary teachers follow elementary curriculum standards and child development principles; middle school teachers follow middle school curriculum standards and adolescent development principles; special education teachers follow individualized education programs and special education standards; career/technical education teachers follow occupational standards and practical training requirements; education administrators follow education policies and school management procedures. Their stages, specialties or management functions differ from this occupation's high school academic teaching.

Main work objects and bases of this occupation | Work with subject, grade and unit topic; learning goals and observable performance; prerequisites and common misconceptions; pedagogy and activity design; assessment tasks and rubrics; and student differences, support and referral requirements. Teach and assess according to curriculum standards, school and subject-team requirements, and student development principles.

Occupational profile | U.S. 25-2031.00 teaches academic subjects at secondary level, excluding special and career/technical education. BLS high school teachers typically teach grades 9—12. This Chinese-language page focuses on general high school subject teaching, combining preparation, assessment, classroom order, student support and home-school collaboration. Do not automatically include private tutoring institutions or special education roles in this statistical occupation.

Core processes of neighboring roles | Elementary teachers focus on general or subject-specific elementary teaching; middle school teachers on middle school subjects; special education teachers on implementing individualized education programs; career/technical education teachers on vocational skills practice; this occupation on high school academic subjects and preparation for further education and graduation.

Core process of this occupation | Receive and check curriculum standards and student learning information; define learning goals and assessment tasks; prepare activities, materials and differentiated support; deliver teaching and maintain order and safety; provide evidence-based feedback and adjustments; and record, collaborate on teaching and communicate with families. Every step must follow curriculum standards and school requirements and be open to review by subject teams, schools and parents.

Main outputs of neighboring roles | Elementary teachers produce evidence of elementary academic development and teaching records; middle school teachers produce evidence of middle school academic development and teaching records; special education teachers produce individualized education program implementation and progress records; career/technical education teachers produce practical training outcomes and skill assessment records. These differ from this occupation's evidence of high school academic development and teaching records.

Main outputs of this occupation | Teaching and assessment completed according to curriculum standards and school requirements: learning goals, activities and assessment tasks; homework, assessments and rubrics; feedback and improvement; and learning progress, attendance, support and referral records. Outputs also include teaching, assessment and curriculum delivery records, parent communication and instructional collaboration records, abnormalities and outstanding items, and traceable unit and term handover records.

Responsibility in neighboring roles | Responsibility in related and neighboring roles is usually defined by the school, education authorities, teacher professional ethics and safety procedures, primarily concerning student development, academic fairness, campus safety and educational quality.

Teachers in this occupation are responsible for their own teaching goals, curriculum delivery, assessment, feedback and records, and teaching according to curriculum standards, school requirements and student development principles. Student mental health, safety, special education assessments, legal matters and home-school disputes must be referred under procedures to school psychological services, management or relevant organizations.

Authority and approvals in neighboring roles | Authority comes from teaching qualifications, school appointment and educational administration systems. It usually excludes independent decisions on curriculum structure, assessment systems, student discipline or major responses. Curriculum or assessment system changes, major student actions and legal matters should be referred to the school or education authority.

Authority and approvals in this occupation | Routine teaching goals, activities, assessment, feedback and records must remain within teaching qualifications, school authorization and curriculum standards. Curriculum and assessment system changes, student discipline, psychological crises, safety and legal matters must follow procedures and school or education authority requirements. Teaching, laboratory, activity and special education qualifications and authorization are subject to competent authority and school requirements.

Limits on conclusions in neighboring roles | Conclusions are mostly limited to the relevant subject, educational stage or function and generally do not determine special education assessments, psychological or medical matters, or legal liability. Conclusions spanning specialties or involving major student rights and safety have limits on their applicability.

Limits on conclusions in this occupation | Conclusions on teaching goals, assessment, feedback and records should state only verifiable learning evidence, teaching actions and results, distinguishing measured facts, judgments and inferences, and matters awaiting verification. Teachers must not issue conclusions in their own name beyond their qualifications, such as special education assessments, psychological or medical diagnoses or legal liability determinations.

Base findings on written recruitment information, employment contracts, job descriptions and school procedures, and keep confirming them after joining. paragraphs: Risk boundaries | Editorial failure examples identified from teaching tasks and school procedures, not incidence rates or risk ratings. Teachers observe and report student needs; psychological or medical diagnoses and specialist special education assessments follow relevant professional authority. Direct answer | Central risks extend beyond finishing a lesson to several failure categories with substantial consequences: assessment bias and fairness failures from opaque or inconsistent rubrics; laboratory and activity safety failures from inadequate plans, protection or emergency response; student privacy and data protection failures from improper use or disclosure of personal information, grades and family data; student support failures from missed bullying or psychological crisis signals or delayed referrals; home-school conflict failures from inadequate communication and records; and record and archive failures where missing or inaccurate teaching and assessment records prevent responsibility from being determined.

Evidence scope | This page draws on O*NET 25-2031.00 tasks and work context: preparing students for later grades; teaching through lectures, discussions and demonstrations; establishing and enforcing behavior rules and order procedures; preparing materials and classrooms for activities; and adapting teaching to varying needs and interests. Context includes high assessment accuracy requirements, serious consequences from erroneous or biased assessments and safety omissions, substantial responsibility for student health and safety, and time pressure from lessons, examinations and grading milestones. entries.answer: This page's Secondary School Teachers, Except Special and Career/Technical Education is the exact O*NET occupation 25-2031.00: teaching one or more subjects to secondary-level students. The page lists 32 tasks. The most important include preparing students for later grades; teaching subjects through lectures, discussions and demonstrations; establishing and enforcing student behavior rules and procedures for maintaining order; preparing materials and classrooms for activities; and adapting teaching methods and materials to varying needs and interests. Common job titles include High School Teacher, Secondary Teacher, Math Teacher and English Teacher.

subject.summary: This page covers the exact O*NET/SOC occupation 25-2031.00, Secondary School Teachers, Except Special and Career/Technical Education: teaching one or more subjects to students at the secondary school level. Core tasks include preparing students for later grades; teaching one or more subjects through lectures, discussions and demonstrations; establishing and enforcing student behavior rules and procedures for maintaining order; preparing materials and classrooms for activities; and adapting teaching methods and materials to students' varying needs and interests. Common job titles include High School Teacher, Secondary Teacher, Math Teacher, English Teacher and Science Teacher. Official scope: Teach one or more subjects to students at the secondary school level. Coverage note: U.S. wage, employment and industry data presented on O*NET's 25-2031.00 page are not marked as coming from a broader or neighboring occupation, and only annual wages are provided. This page identifies them as data for this occupation itself (25-2031.00). The occupation is in Job Zone Four (considerable preparation needed), 7.0 to less than 8.0 (SVP 7.0 to < 8.0), with Decline growth (-1% or lower) for 2024—2034. This page does not constitute educational, assessment, safety, psychological or legal advice.
